title: Founder Ji Shisan Says Science and Education Can Both Make Money for Guokr
excerpt: Guokr, which made its name in popular science, is now incubating more products in the fields it knows best, and has gradually shaken off outside doubts about its business model.
body:
Guokr, which made its name in popular science, is now incubating more products in the fields it knows best, and has gradually shaken off outside doubts about its business model.

Even in LangYuan Vintage, a creative-industry park in Beijing, Guokr, a general-interest science community, stands out. Last week we met its founder and CEO, Ji Xiaohua, better known as Ji Shisan, at the office. That afternoon the place was unusually quiet: nobody scrambling for the afternoon-tea fruit, nobody recording a podcast in a meeting room, nobody playing a nostalgic round of *The King of Fighters* on the coin-operated arcade machine by the back door.

In 2008, Ji Shisan, who had been writing for traditional media, joined a group of science writers to found a group blog called the "Science Squirrels" (Kexue Songshuhui). Once it added offline events, it became a non-profit organization. But the Squirrels were still some way from the professional science and technology media outlet Ji had in mind, and the strongest push toward that goal would come from a business model. In 2010, after taking angel investment from Zhixin Capital, Ji founded Guokr as a commercial company. The move was not easy to explain, especially since the two organizations shared so many of the same writers.

Some have likened Zhihu and Guokr to two "eggs" laid in China by the knowledge community Quora: the first "took its form" and became an excellent platform for people to share experience; the second "took its spirit" and built an idealistic science-communication community. But the two companies faced the same doubt about their business models: can a huge user base and a good reputation be turned into steady cash flow?

In [an earlier QDaily interview](http://qdaily.com/display/cards/7672.html), Zhihu CEO Zhou Yuan said Zhihu would make its money from native advertising. According to Guokr COO Yao Di, speaking at the company's third-anniversary event, brand marketing alone brought Guokr 5 million yuan in 2012 and 10 million yuan in 2013. She added a quip: "Nowhere near as fast as Ji Shisan spends it."

Ji went through a corporate transition in mid-2012 and was unsure of his direction for a while. He now believes the community's original core users are not enough: "If you look at science purely as popular science, it really is a very small thing. But if you look at science as popular culture, that's another matter altogether. Science fiction is the same: how many people actually read science fiction novels? And how many watch science fiction blockbusters?"

Over the past year, the company has built more stand-alone products along two broad lines, science and education, trying to win over ordinary people who "identify with the scientific spirit," or who "think science is awesome." Every three months, the executive team sits down to go through a pile of new product ideas from inside the company. Then, in more frequent day-to-day discussions, it decides whether each product should expand, hold steady, change course or pause.

This multi-product approach has drawn more questions from users. Why is Guokr, still a startup, turning itself into a product incubator? Why enter the fiercely competitive education market when it is already good at science communication? How does the company manage all these freely growing new products? And beyond brand marketing, what new ways of making money will they create?

We put these questions to Ji Shisan. Here are his answers:

### Four Years On, Why Has Guokr Become a Product Incubator?

Q: Guokr is now more than four years old. How has it changed along the way?

A: I think Guokr has gone through a few stages. The first was in 2010, when we had just started. The idea then was to build a new-media outlet for science. Could science be commercialized? How could science communication be combined with a product business model? When we started, we weren't very clear on that. So although things look fairly good now, we made some mistakes along the way.

From 2012 we began looking for change, and you could see Guokr change a lot and try many new things. From the outside, Guokr seemed to have one new product, then another new thing, then another. That was us looking for change.

Then, as a new round of financing came onto the agenda, from the second half of 2014 onward, the company's thinking became much clearer over the course of the process. Today our business has two parts: science and education. There may be new growth within these two areas, of course, but that is the overall direction.

Q: Why did you end up choosing science and education?

A: Looking back at all the things Guokr has done, you find that what we did most successfully, and what we are good at, is closely tied to these two things. If the team is keen to do something that strays too far from these two main lines, it becomes very hard going.

So science and education are less a decision about where to go than a description of where we have been. Looking back, you'll see we have only ever done things related to these two broad areas.

**Q: Over the past year Guokr has launched many small stand-alone products. What was the thinking behind this strategy?**

A: The process is a bit like internal entrepreneurship. There is a lot of creative energy inside the company, and people's ideas need an outlet. At the same time, outside the company, startups are very hot. If we didn't channel these ideas, we would end up losing talent and good resources to the outside.

Starting in 2013, the company broke up its old departmental structure and reorganized around projects. Each project has a full team of 20 to 30 people running a stand-alone product. We set up a review committee. Every three months everyone gets a chance: if you have an idea, you can bring it to the meeting for discussion, and if it passes, the company backs it with internal resources. It's just like starting a business.

![Guokr's office](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702104749VpW0awFMC7yDScm4.jpg-w600)

Q: Who sits on this review committee? And what are its criteria?

A: The committee has five members: me, the COO, the CTO, the head of editorial and the head of business development. But any employee can come and listen, and pick holes on the spot.

Our criteria are much the same as those a big company would use to judge an outside startup: how well the idea fits the company's existing resources, what the return on investment is, and whether it is of value to the company.

Q: Once a new project is approved internally, how is it managed day to day?

A: If it's a small project with nothing yet but an idea, the person who proposed it can lead a team inside the company to develop it. We take a hands-off approach, and the project lead has a lot of decision-making power. For some small projects, we don't strictly review them every three months either; decisions can be made in everyday conversation.

Q: Of the new projects that came out of the company over the past year, which do you find most interesting?

A: At the end of 2014 we made a "City Species Calendar." It started as a small spin-off product we designed with a corporate client, but it turned out to be a surprise hit. So this year we gave the colleague who ran that project more authority, and she can pull together staff internally to do more projects like it.

The "Quantum Bricks" we are about to launch (note: small Lego-style building toys similar to nanoblock, [now on sale](http://detail.koudaitong.com/show/goods?alias=omni55f0)) were made by this team. Depending on how they sell, we may turn this into a whole product line and keep releasing all kinds of cultural and creative products with a science-and-technology angle.

![Guokr's Quantum Bricks building toys](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702104749pkX8GxUyOjzSK7nH.jpg-w600)

Q: Why do you think small things like calendars and Quantum Bricks can be built into a product line?

A: From that accident we found some patterns we can repeat, and we think it is really a matter of fan economics. Over the years Guokr has built up a large number of fans, and when you release something that matches what they want, their buying power is quite striking.

We are still experimenting here. If we make cultural and creative products, what exactly should they look like? How should we price them? We also worked with Quwan on an air purifier called "Xiaodan" (Little Egg), which counts as a smart hardware product. But because it was priced high, at 2,000 yuan, users were more cautious about buying it.

### Only a Clear Business Model Turns Peripheral Users Into Real Users

Q: Where do Guokr's fans mainly come from?

A: At its core, Guokr is still a science website. We don't expect hundreds of millions of users to browse a fairly niche site every day; when you think about it, that's unlikely. But for products like the calendar, most users will certainly come from Weibo and WeChat.

We moved into social media very early and did it well. Our main Weibo account, @Guokr, now has 3.7 million followers, and our sub-accounts and affiliated accounts have nearly 10 million between them; our main WeChat account has more than 800,000 followers. These people may not visit science websites as often as core users do, but they know the Guokr brand well and like it, so when one of our creative products matches what they imagine the brand to be, they will buy it.

I think only when you have worked out how to make money will those peripheral users truly become your users. Until then, they are no different from anyone else.

Q: When did you work this out?

A: I've always felt that a science website can only have so many users. If my user base grew tenfold, it would certainly not be the Guokr of today, and the brand would no longer feel right. So if I want to keep that feel, I have to find other ways.

Guokr's answer is two paths. First, raise the value of strategic users, which is the education business we are building now; in that model, a user is worth far more than in the community. Second, find ways to activate our social groups and turn peripheral users into my users too.

The community and the social groups correspond to Guokr's core users and peripheral users respectively. Our core users will always be few. They are more loyal and share more uniform values: for example, they don't believe in traditional Chinese medicine and aren't afraid of genetically modified food. Peripheral users are different. They may be less loyal, but there are far more of them, and they have commercial value too.

Born in the community, made in the groups: that is what Guokr has been doing these past few years.

Q: What is the ratio between the core users and peripheral users you mention?

A: I'd say one to several dozen, even one to a hundred. Guokr's core users may number in the millions, right? But peripheral users should be in the tens of millions, or even over a hundred million. In China, the number of people who approve of science, who approve of the scientific spirit, or who think science is awesome must be astronomical.

Science fiction is the same: how many people actually read science fiction novels? And how many watch science fiction blockbusters? That's the periphery versus the core, but you have to find ways to bring in the people who watch science fiction.

A science community is like that too. If you look at science purely as popular science, it really is a very small thing. But if you look at science as popular culture, that's another matter.

![Ji Shisan, founder and CEO of Guokr](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702104750RcP0K5u7AfxTzEbZ.jpg-w600)

Q: Last year the content of Guokr's core main site got a new name, **"Scientists" (Kexueren)**. Was that a brand upgrade?

A: In fact, much of what relates to the Guokr brand is highly scientific, but we wanted to separate some related products by audience: some aimed at the general public, some at core users.

The "Scientists" brand is aimed at core users. We position it as China's *Scientific American*: the articles should be of that quality, but in a more internet-native form. So you'll see plenty of analysis of research papers, first-hand pieces written by researchers, and interviews with leading scientists. We hope it will attract genuinely expert science enthusiasts and serve them.

In April this year, Guokr appointed 40 scientists who are highly accomplished in their fields as scientific advisers to "Scientists," which will further raise the quality of its content. "Scientists" also works with top journals such as *Nature*, and is running surveys of the research community, in the hope of helping to solve a few real problems in the field.

Q: Besides Scientists, Guokr once ran a Q&A community. Does your current multi-product strategy affect existing products like that?

A: Guokr Q&A launched, I think, at the end of 2011. Zhihu was still small then, and we thought the idea was worth a try. It wasn't only us; many niche sites were doing Q&A at the time. But after trying it for a while, we found it really was hard. We had one small team in the company doing it, while Zhihu had its entire founding team on it. We covered one niche, Zhihu covered everything, so there was no comparison.

And as Zhihu grew, users' habits and the ways they used these products changed. People turn to the bigger platform first when they want to ask a question, so niche platforms get badly squeezed. Unless you invest heavily, it's hard to make it a stronger product.

Guokr Q&A is now in maintenance mode, looked after by a team of a few people, and our expectations for it are lower than before. You shouldn't spread your effort across ten mediocre products. You should focus on one product that will take off with a little push, and we are always looking for opportunities like that.

### "Doing Some Things We're Not Good At, and Doing Them Fast"

Q: When did you realize that education was another field, besides science, where Guokr might take off?

A: In 2012 we made some small-scale attempts. They didn't produce the results we had hoped for, but they gave us an insight: sharing knowledge and learning knowledge are really side A and side B of the same thing; the only difference is whether you look at it from the side of the person passing it on or the person receiving it. And the two sides share the same business model and the same user value.

Our earlier attempt was an online group where students could discuss what they learned in class, but after a month it had no users. So I used an event as an excuse to go and stay at Tsinghua University for a few days. There I found that after class, students just talked in their dorm rooms, and the top student in each room could basically answer everyone's questions. They had no need to discuss things online.

But at the time another group on our site, called the MOOC Study Room, was quite popular, and it caught our attention. It was popular because Chinese students taking MOOCs then rarely knew anyone around them taking the same course, so they had to go online. So in 2013 we decided to come back into education through MOOCs.

Q: But companies like NetEase had already been doing open courses for some time by then.

A: Yes, but our thinking was that we are good at user-generated content, so we should use that strength to build a community platform and compete by being different.

Another way we differed: many people then were focused on China, but we would go global. In the short term, Chinese educational content still lagged foreign content in quality, and the overseas platforms were scattered. At that moment, a Chinese-language community that brought them together would be valuable.

Take Coursera. At first they also partnered with NetEase and set up a small official platform there. Inside our team, everyone said: we're done for, they're already so closely partnered, is what we're doing worth anything? I said don't worry. On their side it's one team under NetEase's education department; on ours, the CEO himself is leading you. That's a different level of commitment, and so is the value we can offer users.

After our team of a few dozen people had worked on it for a month or two, a great many Chinese students studying on Coursera did come to us to discuss and exchange ideas. Once you have a partnership with an industry leader like that, other platforms are bound to notice you. Our partnership with Khan Academy now, for example, has gone very smoothly.

Q: How much of the company's effort did it take to land the Coursera partnership?

A: Not many people, perhaps, but at the time it took up a large part of my own time and energy.

I remember that at the end of 2013 I went to Orlando in the United States for a NASA space camp event. When I got there, others on the team said, since you're in the US anyway, why not pay them a visit while you're there? So I bought a plane ticket on the spot and flew to San Francisco to visit Coursera's headquarters, having emailed them urgently the day before to set up a meeting.

That meeting didn't go especially well, but it showed we were serious about Coursera. Coursera sees itself as a social enterprise, and when choosing partners it looks for companies whose mission and values are close to its own. Foreigners' trust takes a long time to build, and throughout that process we were willing to treat every chance to work with a course platform seriously.

Q: In education, how does Guokr plan to make money from its users?

A: People now generally accept that education is a business where each customer spends more, and that a great deal of educational content will move online, so there shouldn't be a problem.

We are still working out the business model for [MOOC Academy](http://mooc.guokr.com), and nobody is in a hurry to make money from it right away. We may try a few approaches. One is a share of the fees for certificates; on this, Guokr is currently Coursera's only commercial partner in China. Another is to work with companies to design full sets of hands-on projects that combine coursework with career development, so learners can earn co-branded certificates that also help them find jobs.

![Guokr's MOOC Academy](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702104750BqdtwQoklVMfvZg2.jpg-w600)

Q: Another new Guokr product that has drawn attention recently is **"Zaihang," a platform for booking people to meet and talk**. Why build a product so far removed from both science and education?

A: That also goes back to my stay at Tsinghua. I found that for students, what they study matters less; what matters more is why they are studying it. The ones who had answered that question all did well, because they had a strong sense of purpose and could pick the most important things to learn. But students struggle to make judgments on their own at critical moments. If someone ten years older, who took the same path and has the relevant experience, gives you some guidance, that's worth a great deal.

At the time I was still thinking purely in internet terms, and I felt this product would be too hard to build as a community, so I set it aside. But in 2014 I realized it should be an O2O (online-to-offline) model, and it immediately made sense. So from the second half of that year we ran several rounds of small-scale tests, and the pool of "experts" (hangjia) widened from company employees to people one and two steps removed from us.

We also made some trade-offs along the way. When Guokr does things offline, what it does best is hobby and interest activities, where the team has a great many contacts, so at first our thinking leaned that way. But judging by actual bookings, interest topics drew praise but few buyers, whereas when I listed myself to talk about starting a business, I was hugely popular.

When the first version of Zaihang came out, it didn't work well on some low-end phones. One user who booked me through Zaihang had to uninstall and reinstall the app every day to keep in touch with me. The app is in much better shape now, of course, and since we opened up applications to become an expert, it covers far more fields.

So I made a call then: we would do some things we're not good at, and do them fast, such as career advice.

### How Does Guokr Make Money?

Q: At the end of 2014, Guokr announced a Series C round of US$20 million, of which US$15 million was a strategic investment from TAL Education. Why did you choose them?

A: When TAL first approached us, they didn't know we were doing education; they just felt our user bases overlapped heavily. They do K-12 education (note: primary and secondary schooling), while we serve university students and graduates interested in science, and on top of that we had a MOOC business that was going fairly well. The two sides hit it off at once.

Q: Did Guokr make any specific commitments to TAL, or to earlier investors such as Zhixin and IDG?

A: Nothing special. The people who invest in us are mostly looking at long-term growth and don't expect much in the way of financial returns.

Q: What is the company's main source of revenue at the moment?

A: The more traditional one is integrated marketing for science and technology brands broadly. The ones we are developing are those we mentioned earlier: sales of cultural and creative products, making money from content, and some experiments in education.

Q: How does Guokr choose which brands to work with?

A: Our bar is quite high. If you listed all the brands we've worked with, they would basically be Fortune 500 companies plus some top-tier Chinese brands. We are also careful. Although brand marketing is mainly handled by the business department, our site's editor-in-chief, Muji, has a veto over these projects. Around 80% of all proposed projects have been turned down for one reason or another, because, first, taking on too many projects hurts the quality of each one, and second, the risk goes up too.

Q: Is there a company you see as Guokr's model?

A: Not really. The only close one is that in 2010 we talked loudly about becoming China's Discovery, because we really like that media company. The same goes for *Scientific American*; their position and products were fairly close to ours at the time.

But the creativity and innovation happening in Beijing and Shenzhen now far outstrip what's happening abroad. Beijing, for example, has become, like Silicon Valley, one of the fastest-growing and most innovative places in the world, and no other country or city can match it. What we are doing now, Zaihang and MOOC Academy, are business models that are new anywhere in the world, and in future others may copy us. One phrase I rather agree with is C2W: China to World.

Q: How many employees does the company have in total? And how do you evaluate performance internally?

A: About 120 full-time employees. Half work on science, including the editorial department, the community, knowledge and business departments; on its own, that half would already be a small, profitable company. The other half work on education and on incubating new products.

We mainly rely on OKRs (objectives and key results) for team management and coordination; all the trendy companies use them now. We brought them in a year ago, and each project has its own objectives.

![Guokr's office](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702104751hJWvQf3Id5yVGHqm.jpg-w600)

Q: What do you value most when hiring?

A: It depends on the role. The main thing is whether their skills fit, and on that basis we may look at values and culture. A science editor who flatly and blindly rejects genetic modification, for example, might not work out, but for a more general role such as receptionist, we don't ask as much of their science background.

Q: Which phone apps have you been using a lot lately? And do you still read, or take MOOCs?

A: Lately I've been using a lot of O2O apps, mostly because of our projects. As for books, I read all sorts of things at random. As for MOOCs, I haven't kept them up.

Q: What will Guokr do next?

A: In education we will keep pushing ahead, and MOOC Academy will change a lot. Zhixing and Zaihang will be spun off as projects that Guokr incubates and that raise money and grow separately. In science, there's the testing of cultural and creative products I mentioned, and later we will also work with other organizations to provide services for science startups.

*QDaily will keep following companies like this: ones that may have been around for a while and won a good reputation among users and a real voice in their industries, but that cannot yet be called big companies. For these companies, which keep their startup spirit but have begun to scale, we will look at what they plan to do next and what they are thinking about now.*
